In most allowable-costs frameworks, especially U.S. federal grants under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200, Subpart E, which opens with §200.400 "Policy guide"), the "policy statement" is the overarching set of principles that governs every charge to an award, as distinct from the item-by-item rules on specific costs. Under the federal cost principles for institutions of higher education (2 CFR 200, Appendix III, which carries forward the former OMB Circular A-21), sponsored instruction and training is specific instructional or training activity established by a grant, contract, or cooperative agreement with an external sponsor. Examples include federally funded training grants, fellowship and traineeship programs, and sponsored curriculum or course development projects. For F&A rate purposes, it may be treated as a separate major function with its own rate, even if the institution's accounting records place it within the general instruction function. Instruction funded by the institution's own resources, such as regular credit courses paid for with tuition or general funds, is not sponsored instruction, nor is departmental research that is not separately budgeted and accounted for.

CSULB's Timely Graduation for Undergraduates policy (PS 10-06), recommended by the Academic Senate on April 29, 2010 and approved by the president on May 17, 2010, aims to ensure timely graduation so that as many qualified students as possible can access undergraduate programs. Most Financial Conflict of Interest (FCOI) policies at research institutions implement the U.S. Public Health Service regulations at 42 CFR Part 50, Subpart F (and 45 CFR Part 94 for contracts), which aim to keep federally funded research free from bias caused by investigators' financial interests. Investigators must disclose significant financial interests related to their institutional responsibilities, generally income or equity above $5,000 from an entity, any equity in a non-publicly traded company, intellectual property income, and sponsored or reimbursed travel. They must disclose before applying for funding, at least annually, and within 30 days of acquiring a new interest. A designated institutional official reviews these disclosures to decide whether a conflict exists. If one does, the institution must manage, reduce, or eliminate it through a management plan and report it to the funding agency (such as NIH), and investigators must also complete FCOI training at least every four years. Your institution's specific policy may differ in its details, so check its own policy document for exact thresholds and procedures.

Under CSULB's PS 19-03, reassigned time releases faculty from other duties to pursue research, scholarly, and creative activity (RSCA), while faculty small grants are monetary awards that can cover expenses like student assistance, minor equipment, materials and supplies, or RSCA-related travel. Both are awarded competitively at the college level, using Academic Affairs allocations that colleges may supplement with their own funds. Awards may take the form of reassigned time, small grants, or a combination, equivalent to the Vacant Rate for up to 6 WTU per academic year. Requests above 3 WTU require additional justification, and awardees receiving more than 3 WTU of reassigned time may take it in one semester or spread it over two. College faculty councils set the application and evaluation criteria, procedures, and deadlines, determine the award committee's composition and charge, and may establish procedures for converting reassigned time into small grants and vice versa.

At CSULB, Retention, Tenure, and Promotion (RTP) timelines are set by the CSU–CFA collective bargaining agreement (primarily Article 15) together with the campus RTP policy and the department and college RTP documents. Each year Faculty Affairs publishes an RTP calendar with fixed deadlines for closing the file (usually in early fall), for each level of review (department committee, chair, college committee, dean, and provost), and for final notification. Probationary faculty are typically reviewed for retention during the probationary period and considered for tenure in the sixth year, though service credit or early consideration can change this. At each review level, the candidate receives a copy of the recommendation and has a set period, generally 10 days under the CBA, to submit a written response or rebuttal or to request a meeting before the file moves on. Because exact dates change annually, you should check the current Faculty Affairs RTP calendar and your department's RTP policy.

Under CSULB Academic Senate Policy Statement 73-03 (March 4, 1974), non-matriculating students may enroll in regular program classes by paying extension fees, provided there is insufficient enrollment to develop an extension class and the department concerned grants permission. Funds from concurrent enrollment are divided as follows: 25 percent to the Continuing Education Reserve Fund, 50 percent to supporting departments on a pro rata basis, and 25 percent to the Office of Continuing Education for operating expenses. The policy also incorporates Chancellor's Office rules: extension students cannot justify continuing a low-enrollment class, take a place from a resident student, or be a reason for splitting a class. Concurrent enrollment should cause no loss to the Continuing Education Revenue Fund, which must keep a reasonable percentage to cover indirect costs, and any revenue beyond what extension needs to run the program may be spent for other University purposes.

Under CSULB's University RTP Policy (PS 23-24), all tenure-track and tenured faculty undergo performance review: tenure-track faculty are evaluated every year, with a periodic review in years without reappointment, tenure, or promotion review, and tenured faculty are evaluated every five years. In many university and public-institution "Time, Place and Manner" policies, the "Kiosks" section governs designated physical structures, such as freestanding bulletin boards or posting pillars, where people may put up flyers, posters, and other printed notices. I don't know which institution's Policy on Student Media you mean, so I can't quote its exact wording, but these sections usually follow a common pattern. Most U.S. college student media policies bar publishing material that is legally "obscene" and rely on the Supreme Court's *Miller v. California* (1973) test. Under that test, material is obscene only if it appeals to a prurient interest in sex by contemporary community standards, depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Because of that narrow definition, such policies typically make clear that content that is merely vulgar, profane, offensive, or controversial is still protected and isn't grounds for censorship.
